summary.text: Case 1: A 76-year-old woman was referred to gastroenterology after 15 months of progressively worsening postprandial abdominal discomfort, bloating, diarrhea and early satiety with 27 kg unintentional weight loss. Prior upper and lower endoscopies and abdominal CT were non-diagnostic; she had hypertension/hyperlipidemia, no significant GI-family history, benign abdominal exam without peritonitis or masses, and mildly elevated fecal calprotectin (250 mg/kg) with other normal labs.

Earlier abdominal CT was re-reviewed by the gastroenterology registrar, revealing previously unreported SMA/celiac origin calcification. Dedicated CTA confirmed high-grade SMA stenosis. A 1.5 cm SMA occluded segment was described as suspected in the initial CTA wording and more definitively in the same-study figure description; her quiescent GCA without steroids for over a decade prompted rheumatology/PET-CT review, both negative for reactivation. The authors describe a diagnostic delay of over a year despite prior evaluations.

CMI due to SMA atherosclerosis was diagnosed. Vascular surgery referral led to successful percutaneous angioplasty/stenting, with patent SMA and good distal filling on completion angiography. At 11 months she had regained approximately 5 kg and post-prandial pain resolved; the report describes full GI symptom resolution.

summary.text: Case 2: A 71-year-old woman was referred to gastroenterology after 12 months of progressive vague upper abdominal pain, early satiety and diarrhea with 12 kg weight loss. Prior GI workup was non-diagnostic; she had hypertension/hyperlipidemia, no significant GI-family history, benign abdominal exam without peritonitis or masses, and unremarkable labs.

Earlier abdominal CT was re-reviewed by the gastroenterology registrar, revealing previously unreported SMA/celiac origin calcification. Dedicated CTA confirmed high-grade SMA stenosis. Extensive calcification ran along the SMA; she also had prior symptomatic PAD treated by right common iliac stenting 13 years earlier. The authors describe a diagnostic delay of over a year despite prior evaluations.

CMI due to SMA atherosclerosis was diagnosed. Vascular surgery referral led to successful percutaneous angioplasty/stenting, with patent SMA and good distal filling on completion angiography. At 6 months she had regained approximately 8 kg and post-prandial pain resolved; the report describes full GI symptom resolution.
